newsitem.title: UK: Ecu surfs EMU euphoria as legal confusion beached.
newsitem.headline: Ecu surfs EMU euphoria as legal confusion beached.

text.p: The European currency unit caught the crest of this week's tidal wave of optimism about a punctual start for European monetary union and rode to its highest level in almost two years against a sinking mark.
Profit-taking emerged to sweep the Ecu off these highs earlier today but interest in the unit's potential remains high.
The Ecu's breather was also related to talk of European cental bank sales of Ecu for marks, which may be aimed at preventing an undesirable wipeout of the German currency.

However, while the Ecu's high watermark may have been set for now, a clearing of the mist surrounding the Ecu's legal status still makes it one of the more attractive so-called "convergence trades" left to play, said analysts.
"The Ecu/mark move has been an interesting trade this week and has outperformed most of the currencies on the EMU story," said Andrew Chaveriat, analyst at Banque Paribas.
The Ecu/mark rate rose two percent since early August to a peak of 1.9125 marks on Thursday, its highest level since October 1994. At 1330 GMT, it was at 1.9070/75.
"If you buy in the convergence trade idea, many rates were already quite expensive," said Chaveriat. "Rather than pick a horse that's already run too quickly, the Ecu looked better value."
Analysts said a renewed scramble for convergence has intensified the hunt for best-value buys, based on the increasingly entrenched belief in a 1999 start for EMU.
Convergence trades bet on locking into relatively high, but falling, yields in times of reduced currency risk.

The Ecu, which originated as a basket of the 12 original European Union currencies and was for years proposed as the eventual single currency, has also been given added buoyancy of its own in recent weeks.
It now looks almost certain that there will be a legal guarantee to exchange existing Ecus for the new single currency, or euro, on a one-for-one basis, analysts said.

European finance ministers meeting in Dublin last weekend agreed that clarification of legal issues relating to the single currency, such as the guarantee of one-for-one conversion of the existing Ecu contracts with the new euro, should be a priority.

As a result, they said Article 235 of the Maastricht Treaty will allow such urgent legal decisions, which cannot wait until the EMU launch to be clarified, to be dealt with providing there is unanimity among the 15 EU states. The European Commission is due to put forward a paper on the issue in mid-October for formal adoption at the EU summit in December.

Growing optimism about EMU and the rising hopes for a prompt legal clarification of the Ecu's status lowered the discount with which market-traded Ecu trades to its theoretical value, derived from the 12 constituent units. The spread fell from almost one percent last week to as low as 0.25 percent Thursday.
This is a closely watched indicator of EMU sentiment and a move to par, which has not been seen since early 1993, would signal an extremely high degree of confidence in the project.

"We would expect the spread to compress toward par in the weeks ahead but, theoretically, if we get a hard core monetary union at first, the market Ecu should trade at a premium rather than a discount to the basket," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.

A monetary union between a core of six-to-eight countries would make the euro, with which the Ecu will most likely be swapped one-for-one, a much stronger, more credible unit than the theoretical Ecu basket of 12.
